words.definition: to go up and down often
words.example: Petrol prices {fluctuate} from week to week, rising one week and falling the next.

words.definition: slowly and evenly, without stopping
words.example: The population grew {steadily}, by about one per cent every year.

words.definition: suddenly and by a large amount
words.example: Sales fell {sharply}, by half in a single day, when the news broke.

words.definition: the highest point or level
words.example: Visitor numbers reach their {peak} in August.

words.definition: a gradual fall in amount or quality
words.example: Pesticides have caused a sharp {decline} in the number of bees.

words.definition: about; not exactly
words.example: The journey takes {approximately} three hours.

words.definition: a part of a whole, compared with the total
words.example: A large {proportion} of students walk to school.

words.definition: to become twice as big
words.example: With all the new houses, our town's population could {double} in ten years.

words.definition: to fall very fast and very far
words.example: In some deserts, temperatures can {plummet} after sunset, falling by over twenty degrees overnight.

words.definition: a general direction in which things are changing
words.example: The graph shows a clear upward {trend}: sales have risen every year since 2010.

words.definition: a mistake or weakness that makes something less good or less correct
words.example: The test showed a {flaw} in the bridge's design, so engineers had to strengthen it.

words.definition: something you believe is true without proof
words.example: You made the {assumption} that I was busy, but you never actually asked me.

words.definition: a false belief, or a mistake in reasoning
words.example: In debates, people often commit the {fallacy} of attacking the speaker, not the argument.

words.definition: able to be believed or trusted
words.example: Her story was {credible}: it was easy to believe, and later it turned out to be true.

words.definition: based on facts and not on personal feelings
words.example: A referee must be {objective} and not take sides.

words.definition: based on personal feelings and tastes
words.example: Whether a painting is beautiful is {subjective}.

words.definition: doubt about whether something is true
words.example: Treat claims about miracle cures with {scepticism}.

words.definition: a possible result or effect of something
words.example: If the study is right, one {implication} is that doctors must change how they treat colds.

words.definition: to form an opinion from the facts you have
words.example: The ending is never stated, so readers must {infer} it from small clues.

words.definition: a connection between two things that change together
words.example: There is a strong {correlation} between smoking and lung disease.

words.definition: the decision of a jury or judge at the end of a trial
words.example: The jury reached a {verdict} after three days.

words.definition: the person in court who is accused of a crime
words.example: In court, the {defendant} denied stealing the car.

words.definition: the punishment that a judge gives
words.example: He received a {sentence} of two years in prison.

words.definition: to accuse someone officially of a crime in a court
words.example: The shop will {prosecute} anyone caught stealing.

words.definition: a request to a higher court to change a decision
words.example: Her lawyer has started an {appeal} against the decision.

words.definition: laws, or the process of making laws
words.example: Parliament passes {legislation}, and the courts decide how to apply it.

words.definition: fair treatment by the law
words.example: The families want {justice}: a fair trial and proper punishment for the guilty driver.

words.definition: to decide officially in court that someone is guilty
words.example: The jury did not {convict} him because there was not enough proof.

words.definition: permission for an accused person to stay out of prison until their trial, often with conditions
words.example: The accused is out on {bail} until his trial next month but must report to the police weekly.

words.definition: a person forced to leave their country, for example because of war
words.example: The {refugee} camp is home to ten thousand families.

words.definition: a serious lack of food in a large area
words.example: After years without rain, millions went hungry during the {famine}.

words.definition: helping people who are suffering
words.example: The charity sends {humanitarian} aid after earthquakes.

words.definition: the way the world's economies and cultures are becoming connected
words.example: Through {globalisation}, companies trade across the world, so the same shops appear in Tokyo and Paris.

words.definition: a serious disagreement or a war
words.example: The {conflict} between the two countries lasted ten years and cost thousands of lives.

words.definition: official orders that stop trade with a country
words.example: Several countries imposed {sanctions} on the regime.

words.definition: an agreement to stop fighting
words.example: The two armies agreed to a {ceasefire}, and the fighting stopped at midnight.

words.definition: poorer countries that are building up their industry
words.example: Many {developing countries} still lack clean drinking water.

words.definition: help such as food, money or medicine given to people in need
words.example: Planes carried emergency {aid} to the flooded region.

words.definition: the movement of people or animals from one place to another
words.example: Bird {migration} happens every autumn.

words.definition: a doctor's decision about what illness someone has
words.example: The doctor could not make a {diagnosis} until the blood test showed which illness it was.

words.definition: a substance that protects the body from a disease
words.example: The nurse gave each child the measles {vaccine} with one quick injection in the arm.

words.definition: the parts of the body that fight illness
words.example: Sleep keeps your {immune system} strong enough to fight off colds and flu.

words.definition: lasting a long time
words.example: Asthma is a {chronic} condition: it lasts for years, though attacks come and go.

words.definition: spreading easily from one person to another
words.example: Stay at home while your cold is {contagious}.

words.definition: an unwanted result of taking a medicine
words.example: A common {side effect} of this medicine is feeling sleepy.

words.definition: treatment in which a doctor cuts into the body
words.example: He needed {surgery} on his knee after the fall.

words.definition: a disease that spreads quickly to many people in one area
words.example: The town faced a flu {epidemic} last winter.

words.definition: a medicine that kills bacteria
words.example: The doctor prescribed an {antibiotic} for my ear infection.

words.definition: passed down from parents to children through the body's cells
words.example: Eye colour is mainly {genetic}.

words.definition: the ability to control yourself and make yourself do difficult things
words.example: It takes real {willpower} to put your phone away and study for three hours.

words.definition: a natural way of acting without having to learn or think
words.example: Birds build nests by {instinct}.

words.definition: acting suddenly without thinking first
words.example: Buying a puppy on the way home was an {impulsive} decision.

words.definition: to notice or understand something in a particular way
words.example: Others may {perceive} you as shy, even if you feel confident inside.

words.definition: awake and aware of what is around you
words.example: After the fall, he was still {conscious} and able to talk.

words.definition: a very strong fear of something, often without good reason
words.example: She has a {phobia} of spiders.

words.definition: a quiet person who often prefers to be alone
words.example: As an {introvert}, he prefers small groups to big parties.

words.definition: a lively person who enjoys being with other people
words.example: My sister is a real {extrovert} who loves big parties.

words.definition: to keep delaying something you should do
words.example: I always {procrastinate} when I have an essay to write.

words.definition: the money a company receives from what it sells
words.example: The company's {revenue} from ticket sales rose to two million pounds.

words.definition: the joining of two companies into one
words.example: The {merger} created the country's largest bank.

words.definition: a person who owns part of a company
words.example: As a {shareholder}, she owns a small part of the company.

words.definition: the work of advertising and selling products
words.example: She works in {marketing}, planning adverts that make people want new products.

words.definition: a name that a company gives to its products
words.example: Which {brand} of cereal do you usually buy?

words.definition: the selling of goods to the public in shops
words.example: She has worked in {retail} for years, serving customers in clothes shops.

words.definition: to pay another company to do part of your work
words.example: Many firms {outsource} their customer service to call centres.

words.definition: not able to pay your debts
words.example: The shop went {bankrupt} and closed last year.

words.definition: a new, small company
words.example: She works for a tiny {start-up}: the company is only a year old and has five staff.

words.definition: complete control of a market by one company
words.example: The company has a {monopoly} on trains in the region.

words.definition: a loan used to buy a house or flat
words.example: To buy their flat, they took out a {mortgage} that they will repay over twenty-five years.

words.definition: extra money paid on a loan or on savings
words.example: The bank pays two per cent {interest} on savings.

words.definition: money paid regularly to someone who has stopped working because of age
words.example: Since retiring, my grandad has lived on the {pension} his old employer pays him monthly.

words.definition: paying a company so that it pays you if something bad happens
words.example: Travel {insurance} covers lost luggage.

words.definition: money spent on something, often as part of a job
words.example: Keep your receipts so that the company can pay back your {expenses}.

words.definition: a first payment for something, with the rest paid later
words.example: We paid a {deposit} on the bike and will pay the rest next month.

words.definition: money paid for being taught, especially at university
words.example: Students in England pay {tuition fees} to their university.

words.definition: an amount a bank lets you spend when your account has nothing left in it
words.example: My account was empty, so I paid for the books using my {overdraft}.

words.definition: having a lot of money
words.example: Only {wealthy} families could afford private tutors.

words.definition: a tiny part of your DNA that passes a feature, such as eye colour, from parents to children
words.example: Eye colour depends on more than one {gene}, each a short section of DNA from your parents.

words.definition: the slow change of living things over millions of years
words.example: Fossils help us understand the {evolution} of birds.

words.definition: a living thing
words.example: A bacterium is a tiny {organism} made of a single cell.

words.definition: the smallest living part of a plant or animal
words.example: Under the microscope, we could see each {cell} in the onion skin.

words.definition: a living thing that lives on or in another and takes its food from it
words.example: A flea is a {parasite} that lives on cats and dogs and feeds on their blood.

words.definition: the way plants make food using sunlight
words.example: During {photosynthesis}, leaves take in carbon dioxide.

words.definition: all the living things in an area and the way they depend on each other
words.example: A coral reef is a delicate {ecosystem}.

words.definition: a change in the genes of a living thing
words.example: A random {mutation} gave the moth its dark wings.

words.definition: an animal that hunts and eats other animals
words.example: The fox is a {predator} of rabbits.

words.definition: to change in order to suit new conditions
words.example: Animals must {adapt} to survive in the desert.

words.definition: the force that pulls things towards the ground
words.example: On the Moon, {gravity} is much weaker than on Earth.

words.definition: to travel round a planet or star
words.example: The Earth takes a year to {orbit} the Sun.

words.definition: the force that slows things down when they rub together
words.example: Rubbing your hands together creates {friction} and warmth.

words.definition: speed in a particular direction
words.example: The rocket's {velocity}, its speed in one direction, increased quickly after launch.

words.definition: the smallest part of a chemical element
words.example: A water molecule has one oxygen {atom} and two hydrogen atoms.

words.definition: energy that is sent out as rays
words.example: The Sun's {radiation} can damage your skin.

words.definition: a very small piece of something
words.example: A {particle} of dust floated in the sunlight.

words.definition: a space with no air in it
words.example: Sound cannot travel through a {vacuum}.

words.definition: a huge group of stars
words.example: Our {galaxy} is called the Milky Way.

words.definition: the distance that light travels in one year
words.example: A {light year} is almost ten trillion kilometres.

words.definition: the person who tells a story
words.example: In this novel, the {narrator} tells the story but never takes part in it.

words.definition: the main character in a story
words.example: Most stories have one main character, the {protagonist}, whom the reader follows.

words.definition: describing something as if it were something else
words.example: Saying that time is a thief is a {metaphor}.

words.definition: a comparison that uses "like" or "as"
words.example: "As brave as a lion" is a {simile}.

words.definition: a group of lines in a poem
words.example: The poem has four lines in each {stanza}.

words.definition: a type of book, film or music
words.example: Science fiction is my favourite {genre}.

words.definition: a serious play with a sad ending
words.example: Shakespeare's "Macbeth" is a famous {tragedy}.

words.definition: the time and place in which a story happens
words.example: The {setting} of the novel is a Scottish island in 1900.

words.definition: saying the opposite of what you mean, often to be funny
words.example: With heavy {irony}, he called the rainy day perfect beach weather.

words.definition: morally right or acceptable
words.example: Our school only buys {ethical} chocolate from farmers who are paid fairly.

words.definition: a situation in which you must choose between two difficult options
words.example: She faced a {dilemma}: tell the truth or protect her friend.

words.definition: the feeling inside you that tells you what is right
words.example: I copied my friend's homework, and afterwards my {conscience} made me feel terribly guilty.

words.definition: being honest and having strong principles
words.example: A judge must have {integrity}: she must be honest and never take a bribe.

words.definition: connected with right and wrong
words.example: The fable ends with a {moral} lesson about greed.

words.definition: permission to do something
words.example: You need your parents' {consent} to go on the trip.

words.definition: the freedom to make your own decisions
words.example: Teenagers want more {autonomy} over their own lives.

words.definition: to treat someone unfairly in order to gain from them
words.example: Some factories {exploit} workers by paying them very little.

words.definition: a special advantage that only some people have
words.example: Going to university is a {privilege} that not everyone has.

words.definition: connected with towns and cities
words.example: Cities are growing as more families leave the countryside for {urban} life.

words.definition: connected with the countryside
words.example: Buses are rare in {rural} villages.

words.definition: the roads, railways, pipes and cables that a country needs
words.example: Roads, bridges, railways and power cables are all part of a country's {infrastructure}.

words.definition: with too many people in it
words.example: At rush hour the trains are {overcrowded}, with far too many passengers for everyone to get a seat.

words.definition: an area of houses at the edge of a city
words.example: They moved to a quiet {suburb} outside Manchester.

words.definition: too much traffic on the roads
words.example: Road {congestion} makes the journey twice as long.

words.definition: with homes rather than shops or offices
words.example: The new {residential} block has two hundred flats but no shops or offices.

words.definition: richer people moving into a poorer area and changing it
words.example: As {gentrification} took hold, wealthy newcomers pushed up rents and cheap shops became expensive cafés.

words.definition: buses and trains that everyone can use
words.example: Using {public transport} instead of a car cuts pollution.

words.definition: able to speak a language easily and well
words.example: After a year in Paris, her French was {fluent}; she could chat easily with anyone.

words.definition: a form of a language spoken in one area
words.example: In the north-east, people speak a {dialect} with its own words and grammar.

words.definition: the way your voice goes up and down when you speak
words.example: In English, a rising {intonation} at the end often shows that you are asking a question.

words.definition: able to speak two languages equally well
words.example: Her mum speaks Spanish and her dad speaks English, so she grew up {bilingual}.

words.definition: messages you send by the way you move or stand
words.example: Crossed arms are {body language} that can show you feel defensive.

words.definition: special words used by one group that others find hard to understand
words.example: Doctors' reports are full of medical {jargon}, technical terms that patients rarely understand.

words.definition: very informal words, often used by young people
words.example: Words like 'gonna' are {slang}, so avoid them in formal essays.

words.definition: speaking or writing well and in a way that moves people
words.example: Her {eloquent} speech moved the whole audience.

words.definition: a failure to understand something correctly
words.example: I thought the meeting was at ten, but it was at two: a simple {misunderstanding}.

words.definition: as a result
words.example: The bus was cancelled and, {consequently}, we chose to share a taxi to the match.

words.definition: in spite of that
words.example: It was raining; {nevertheless}, we went for a long walk.

words.definition: in addition to what has been said
words.example: The plan is cheap; {furthermore}, it can be set up in a single afternoon.

words.definition: when compared with others
words.example: Flats here are {relatively} cheap when you compare them with London.

words.definition: in a way that cannot be avoided
words.example: If you invite thirty people, {inevitably} someone will be late; it always happens.

words.definition: used to say that there are good reasons to believe something
words.example: She is {arguably} the best tennis player of her generation.

words.definition: mostly; mainly
words.example: The audience was {predominantly} teenagers.

words.definition: on purpose
words.example: I think he broke the vase {deliberately}, not by accident.

words.definition: completely and carefully
words.example: Wash your hands {thoroughly} before cooking.

words.definition: to suggest something without saying it directly
words.example: He didn't say it directly, but did he mean to {imply} that I was lying?

words.definition: without any break
words.example: This country road has a {continuous} white line down the middle that drivers must not cross.

words.definition: happening again and again, often annoyingly
words.example: I'm tired of your {continual} complaints; you've moaned again and again all day.

words.definition: to make certain that something happens
words.example: Please {ensure} that all windows are closed before you leave.

words.definition: to come before something
words.example: In a storm, lightning will always {precede} thunder, because light travels faster than sound.

words.definition: to continue or go forward
words.example: Passengers for Paris should {proceed} to gate twelve.

words.definition: to go well with something
words.example: The red scarf will {complement} your coat perfectly.

words.definition: something nice said about someone
words.example: She paid me a {compliment} on my new haircut.

words.definition: not moving
words.example: The bus was {stationary}, not moving at all, while the lights were red.
